prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

After love discovers it, the little burn or birthmark in an odd spot he can neither see nor reach; after the internist's downturned mouth, specialists leaning over him like diviners, machines reading his billion cells; after the onslaught of insight, cures crawling through him like infestations, so many surgeries a wrong move leaves him leaking like overripe fruit; after the mountain aster and ice wine, Michigan football, CanesVenatici and the Four North Fracture Zone shrink to a room where voices grow hushed as if at some holy place, and even in the kindest eye there lurks the eternity to which he's been commended; after speech, touch, even the instinct to eat are gone, and he has become nothing but a collection of quiet tics and twitches as if something wanted out of his riddled bones, the carious maze of his brain; as the last day glaciers into his room, glass and chrome so infinites- imally facet- ed it seems he lives inside a diamond, he breaks into a wide smile, as if joy were the animal in him, blind, scrabbling, earth- covered creature tunneling up from God knows where to stand upright, feasting on distances, gazing dead into the sun.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- A hidden mark on the man’s body leads to medical concern and a cascade of examinations by doctors and specialists.
- His illness brings invasive treatments, surgeries, and physical decline that gradually consume his life.
- The vastness of his former world shrinks to a quiet hospital room filled with hushed voices and intimations of death.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: After, Michigan, CanesVenatici

outputs.L1: After love discovers it—the small burn or birthmark in an odd spot he can neither see nor reach; after the internist’s downturned mouth, the specialists leaning over him like diviners, the machines reading his billion cells; after the onslaught of insight, the cures crawling through him like infestations, so many surgeries that a wrong move leaves him leaking like overripe fruit; after the mountain aster and ice wine, Michigan football, Canes Venatici, and the Four North Fracture Zone shrink to a room where voices grow hushed, as if in some holy place, and even in the kindest eye there lurks the eternity to which he has been commended; after speech, touch, and even the instinct to eat are gone, and he has become nothing but a collection of quiet tics and twitches, as if something wanted out of his riddled bones, the carious maze of his brain; as the last day glaciers into his room, the glass and chrome so infinitesimally faceted that it seems he lives inside a diamond, he breaks into a wide smile, as if joy were the animal in him—a blind, scrabbling, earth-covered creature tunneling up from God knows where to stand upright, feasting on distances, gazing dead into the sun.
outputs.L2: Once love notices the small mark—the tiny burn or birthmark hidden where he can neither look at it nor touch it; once the internist gives him that grim, downward pull of the lips, and experts bend above him like people searching for omens, while machines translate the condition of his countless cells; once knowledge arrives in a flood, and treatments move through his body like invading swarms, and there have been so many operations that one careless motion could make him spill open like fruit gone too soft; once mountain asters and ice wine, Michigan football, Canes Venatici, and the Four North Fracture Zone have all narrowed into a single room where people lower their voices as though they are standing in a sacred place, and even the gentlest gaze contains the endlessness he has been handed over to; once language, contact, and even the urge to eat have disappeared, leaving him reduced to a series of faint spasms and tremors, as though some trapped thing is trying to escape his damaged bones and the decayed labyrinth of his mind; as the final day moves slowly into his room, its glass and metal broken into such tiny planes of light that he seems to be living inside a diamond, he suddenly opens into a broad smile, as though joy is the creature still alive within him—a blind, clawing, dirt-covered being burrowing up from some unknown depth to rise on its feet, devour the vast spaces before it, and stare straight into the sun.
outputs.L3:
A hidden mark on the man’s body first draws attention almost by chance, but it soon becomes the beginning of a grave medical concern. What might have seemed small or harmless leads him into a widening circle of examinations, consultations, and uncertainty. Doctors inspect him, specialists are called in, tests are ordered, and his body becomes the subject of anxious interpretation. Each new appointment brings more questions, and each answer seems to lead only to another procedure or diagnosis.

As the illness advances, it begins to dominate every part of his life. Treatments become increasingly invasive, and surgeries leave him weakened and changed. The routines of hospitals, medications, examinations, and recoveries gradually replace the familiar rhythms he once knew. His physical decline is slow but relentless, consuming his strength, narrowing his independence, and making his own body feel less like a source of life than a place of suffering and struggle.

The world he once inhabited—large, varied, and full of movement—contracts around him. What had once included work, family, streets, conversations, and ordinary pleasures is reduced to the stillness of a hospital room. There, the atmosphere is quiet and restrained, filled with hushed voices, careful footsteps, and the unspoken awareness of death. The room becomes a boundary between life and its ending, a place where every sound seems softened by expectation and sorrow.

As his condition worsens, even the most basic forms of expression begin to disappear. Speech leaves him, touch loses its responsiveness, and appetite fades away. He can no longer fully communicate, desire, or participate in the world around him. What remains are small involuntary movements within a body that is failing him: slight gestures, faint shifts, brief signs of life that seem almost separate from will or consciousness. He is gradually reduced to the fragile persistence of the body itself.

Yet on his final day, something unexpected occurs. Despite the nearness of death and the profound decline that has overtaken him, he smiles widely. The smile seems to come from a place deeper than thought or language, a sudden expression of instinctive joy rising from within him. It suggests that even at the edge of life, beyond suffering and loss, some mysterious capacity for happiness remains. In that final moment, death is present, but so is an inexplicable and powerful affirmation of life.
outputs.L4:
The passage portrays a person in the final stages of terminal illness, emphasizing the physical reality of decline through a dense sequence of images. The body is shown as fragile, damaged, and increasingly beyond control: medical details suggest diagnosis, treatment, exhaustion, and the gradual failure of ordinary functions. At the same time, the description is not limited to clinical observation. It moves through sensory impressions—sight, sound, touch, perhaps smell—so that the reader experiences the illness not as an abstract condition but as an immediate, bodily event. The person’s suffering becomes visible in the wasting of the flesh, the weakness of movement, and the atmosphere surrounding the sickroom.

As the imagery develops, the scale of the description expands. What begins as a depiction of one failing body takes on a larger, almost cosmic dimension. The illness is associated not only with hospitals and physical symptoms, but also with images that suggest darkness, dissolution, and the vast forces of nature or the universe. This movement from the medical to the sensory and then to the cosmic makes the individual’s decline feel both intensely personal and universally significant. His body becomes a site where human vulnerability, mortality, and the mystery of existence are all concentrated.

Yet the final moment complicates the scene. Instead of ending only in despair, the text presents the man’s unexpected smile. This smile is striking because it appears in the midst of extreme suffering and bodily collapse. It does not erase the pain or deny the reality of death, but it introduces another force into the passage: a stubborn, instinctive joy. The smile suggests that something in him remains alive, resistant, and unbroken, even when the body is almost defeated. It may be read as a sign of acceptance, defiance, memory, love, or a primal pleasure in existence itself.

Because of this final gesture, the scene rises above a simple account of physical deterioration. The man’s smile gives the moment a transcendent quality, implying that human beings are not defined solely by suffering, illness, or death. Even at the edge of extinction, there can be a flash of vitality that exceeds explanation. The passage therefore presents death not only as degradation, but also as a moment in which the deepest and most mysterious forms of human resilience can appear.
outputs.L5:
After a long winter in Michigan, the night sky feels especially clear and full of promise. Far from the bright city lights, observers can look upward and find the quiet beauty of the constellation Canes Venatici, the “Hunting Dogs,” tucked near Ursa Major. Though it is not one of the most famous constellations, Canes Venatici is home to fascinating deep-sky objects, including the Whirlpool Galaxy.

For anyone in Michigan who enjoys astronomy, spring is a wonderful season to explore this part of the sky. After sunset, when the air grows still and the stars begin to sharpen, Canes Venatici offers a peaceful reminder of how much there is to discover beyond our world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single long, lyrical sentence in the style of a contemporary prose poem about a man dying of cancer, moving from diagnosis and treatment to a final unexpected smile.
counterfactuals.output: When the doctor named the shadow blooming in his blood, he listened as if to weather arriving from another country, then entered the bright machinery of treatment with his sleeves rolled up and his wife’s hand warm in his, the months becoming a calendar of needles, plastic chairs, metallic tastes, prayer cards, sleep, nausea, small stubborn jokes, and windows where the trees kept changing without asking permission, until his body was less a house than a room slowly emptied of furniture, the bed drawn close to the murmuring oxygen, the family gathered like dusk at the edges, and just when grief had already begun rehearsing its heavy music, he opened his eyes, saw something none of them could see, and smiled as though the world, after all its sorrow, had leaned down and told him a secret.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an elegiac paragraph with repeated “after” clauses, dense medical imagery, and cosmic/geological references, ending with a startling image of joy emerging at the moment of death.
counterfactuals.output: After the monitors had worried the dark with their green metronomes, after the IV trees had bloomed their clear, cold fruit, after the lungs filled and emptied like damaged bellows beneath the ribcage’s pale geology, after the blood became a red tide charted by nurses in the archipelago of bruises, after the heart’s small volcano stuttered under its crust of electrodes, after the marrow remembered its ancient salt and the bones lay quiet as moonlit shale, after the tumor’s black star had spent itself in the private galaxy of the abdomen, after the kidneys dimmed like twin planets losing orbit, after every vein had been mapped, punctured, named, forgiven, we stood around the bed as if at the edge of a crater, listening to the body recede into its mineral silence; and then, at the final exhale, when death opened its sterile white door, a laugh—bright, impossible—rose from her mouth like a flock of golden birds bursting out of a grave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary flash fiction passage about terminal illness where the body is described as both machinery and landscape, and the final line suggests transcendence without sentimentality.
counterfactuals.output:
By March, her body had become both factory and field.

The doctors spoke of systems: valves, ducts, pressures, failures. They stood at the foot of the bed with their tablets glowing, as if consulting the dashboard of a stalled machine. Her lungs were bellows worn thin at the hinges. Her heart, a pump working past warranty, knocked unevenly in its housing. Tubes entered her like temporary wiring. Each morning, a nurse adjusted the drip with the precision of a mechanic tuning an engine that no longer cared for the road.

But inside, she felt acreage.

There were gullies where pain had run all night. There were dry creek beds in her arms, blue with distance. Her ribs rose like fence posts from a snowed-in pasture. Beneath the sheet, her legs were two abandoned roads leading nowhere anyone could follow. Sometimes, when the morphine spread its pale weather through her, she imagined weeds taking the hospital room: milkweed at the monitors, thistle in the oxygen ports, moss softening the chrome rails.

Her son read beside her, turning pages too quietly. He had brought oranges, though she could no longer eat them. Their skins shone on the windowsill like small suns left over from another climate.

In the evening, the machines kept their strict little prayers. Beep, hush, click. Beep, hush, click. She listened until the sounds loosened from meaning and became insects in summer grass.

Near midnight, she opened her eyes. Beyond the glass, the city burned in its grids and signals, all that circuitry of longing. She lifted one hand, not to wave, but as if testing for rain.

Then the engine stopped, and the field went on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poetic monologue in one sentence about watching a loved one decline in a hospital room, using surreal metaphors, scientific language, and an ending that turns toward fierce, inexplicable happiness.
counterfactuals.output: In the hospital room where the monitors chirped like trapped green insects and your breath kept negotiating with the cold mathematics of oxygen saturation, I watched you become both star and specimen, a small collapsing galaxy under a cotton blanket, your veins blue rivers on a lunar map, your hands pale hypotheses disproving touch, while the IV drip counted time in transparent planets and the fluorescent lights poured their sterile dawn over everything we had ever loved, until, for no reason the body could justify and no machine could measure, I felt happiness rise in me like a feral sun, bright and brutal and impossible, as if even at the edge of losing you the universe had opened its terrible mouth and begun to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem modeled on high-modernist elegy: include diagnosis, specialists, surgeries, loss of speech and appetite, a bright hospital room, and a final smile described as an animal rising toward the sun.
counterfactuals.output:
In the bright hospital room, noon kept polishing its instruments.

The diagnosis entered first, in a white coat of syllables:  
a name with barbs, a Latin hinge, a small black star  
burning under the tongue. Then came the specialists,  
each carrying a map of the body with one province darkened—  
the throat, the gut, the little gates of breath—  
and spoke in careful weather.

There were surgeries. There were corridors that lengthened  
like arguments after midnight. There were signatures,  
gloved hands, the cold blue theatre of mercy,  
the body opened and closed like a difficult book  
no one could finish reading.

Afterward, speech went out. Not all at once—  
first the consonants, then the bread of vowels,  
then the desire to answer. Appetite followed,  
a shy dog refusing the threshold. The spoon shone.  
The cup waited. The mouth became a room  
where no guest arrived.

Yet light insisted. It stood at the window  
with its gold insistence, touching the sheets,  
the chrome rail, the vase without flowers,  
the face diminished but not defeated.  
Machines counted. Nurses moved softly  
through the hush like figures crossing snow.

We had brought nothing adequate:  
not music, not prayer, not the old stories  
with their ladders of rescue. Only our hands,  
awkward and warm, only our names  
leaning over the bed, only the unbearable art  
of remaining.

Then, near evening, when the walls were filled  
with that clean, pitiless brightness,  
you turned from the far country of pillows  
and gave us one last smile—  
small, deliberate, wild—  
like an animal rising through tall grass toward the sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
